ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A small charged sphere is suspended by an insulating light string of length $l = 0.2 \, \mathrm{m}$. The mass of the sphere is $\mathrm{m} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2} \, \mathrm{kg}$, and the charge it carries is $\mathrm{q} = +2.0 \times 10^{-8} \, \mathrm{C}$. A uniform horizontal electric field is applied, and the region of the electric field is sufficiently large. At equilibrium, the insulating string makes an angle $\theta = 37^{\circ}$ with the vertical direction. It is known that $\mathrm{g} = 10 \, \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, $\sin37^{\circ} = 0.6$, and $\cos37^{\circ} = 0.8$.

1. Find the magnitude of the electric field strength in a uniform electric field.
2. If the light rope is pulled to the right until it is horizontal and then released from rest, find the speed of the small ball when it reaches the lowest point.
3. If the light rope is cut at the position shown in the figure, determine the subsequent motion of the small ball and calculate the magnitude of the ball's velocity after 0.1s.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the upper part of the figure there is a fixed suspension point, and a light string connects the small ball obliquely downward to the right from the suspension point; below the suspension point a vertical dashed line is drawn, and the angle θ between the string and the vertical direction is marked. There are also multiple horizontal arrows pointing to the right in the figure, labeled E, indicating that the direction of the uniform electric field is to the right. A horizontal dashed line is also drawn above, with a small circle at the right end, indicating that the string is pulled to the horizontal rightward position. The position where the string is cut as mentioned in question 3 corresponds to the equilibrium position in the figure where the small ball is at the lower right and the string makes an angle θ with the vertical. Reasoning calculation: 1. At equilibrium the small ball is acted on by three forces: gravity mg downward, electric field force qE to the right, and string tension T along the string pointing toward the suspension point. Decomposing along the vertical and horizontal directions: T cosθ = mg, T sinθ = qE. Dividing the two equations gives tanθ = qE/(mg), so E = mg tanθ / q = mg(sinθ/cosθ)/q. Substituting m = 1.0×10^-2 kg, g = 10 m/s^2, q = 2.0×10^-8 C, sin37°/cos37° = 0.6/0.8 = 0.75: E = (0.01×10×0.75)/(2.0×10^-8) = 0.075/(2.0×10^-8) = 3.75×10^6 N/C. 2. Released from rest from the horizontal rightward position, when reaching the lowest point directly below the suspension point, gravity does positive work mgl, and the electric field force is to the right, while the small ball's horizontal displacement changes from x = l to x = 0, so the work done by the electric field force is qE(0-l) = -qEl. By the kinetic energy theorem: (1/2)mv^2 = mgl - qEl. Also qE = 2.0×10^-8×3.75×10^6 = 0.075 N, mg = 0.10 N, l = 0.2 m, so the net work = (0.10 - 0.075)×0.2 = 0.005 J. Thus (1/2)(0.01)v^2 = 0.005, v^2 = 1, v = 1 m/s. 3. After cutting the string at the equilibrium position shown in the figure, the tension disappears, and the small ball is acted on only by gravity mg downward and the electric field force qE to the right. Because the initial velocity is zero and the resultant force is constant, the small ball undergoes uniformly accelerated straight-line motion along the direction of the resultant force, in the downward-right direction. The acceleration components are ax = qE/m = 0.075/0.01 = 7.5 m/s^2, ay = g = 10 m/s^2 downward, and the magnitude of the resultant acceleration a = sqrt(7.5^2 + 10^2) = 12.5 m/s^2. After 0.1 s the speed magnitude v = at = 12.5×0.1 = 1.25 m/s.
